subject: Chemistry
title: Antibiotic Resistance: Evolution Fights Back
description: A 60-second lesson on Antibiotic Resistance: Evolution Fights Back.

hook.text: Bacteria are evolving faster than we can make antibiotics. Drug-resistant infections kill 1.27 million people yearly.

buildup.text: When antibiotics kill 99.9% of bacteria, the 0.1% that survive carry resistance genes. They multiply and spread.

discovery.text: Bacteria share resistance genes through plasmids—tiny DNA rings passed between cells, even between different species.

twist.text: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) resists most antibiotics. It kills more Americans than HIV each year.

climax.text: Fleming warned in his Nobel speech that misuse would breed resistance. We didn't listen. The post-antibiotic era is approaching.

punchline.text: Evolution outpaces chemistry. Every antibiotic creates pressure for resistance.

quiz.question: How do bacteria spread antibiotic resistance between species?
options: Through plasmids—small DNA rings transferred between bacterial cells
By releasing resistance chemicals into the surrounding environment
Through mutations that occur only during antibiotic treatment

details.summary: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve mechanisms to survive drug exposure, including enzymes that destroy antibiotics, altered target proteins that drugs cannot bind, and efflux pumps that expel drugs from the cell..
details.whyItMatters: The WHO calls antibiotic resistance one of the greatest threats to global health. Over 1.27 million deaths in 2019 were directly attributed to drug-resistant infections, and the number is rising.
takeaways: Bacteria evolve drug resistance through mutation and gene acquisition
Horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance between unrelated species
Overuse and misuse of antibiotics accelerate resistance development

faq.question: How does overuse of antibiotics in agriculture contribute to resistance?
faq.answer: Over seventy percent of antibiotics sold globally are used in livestock, often at sub-therapeutic doses that promote resistance without fully killing bacteria. Resistant bacteria from farms spread to humans through food, water, and direct contact, introducing resistance genes into human pathogens.

faq.question: What happens if we run out of effective antibiotics?
faq.answer: A post-antibiotic era would make routine surgeries, organ transplants, and cancer chemotherapy extremely dangerous. Simple infections could become life-threatening again. The economic cost has been estimated at over one hundred trillion dollars by 2050 if resistance trends continue unchecked.
